User: I'd like to prepare for my annual physical. I'm 55, with COPD (losartan 50mg and amlodipine 5mg), high cholesterol (naproxen as needed), and a history of nephropathy. My PCP is Dr. Maria Santos at Seattle Endocrinology. My last FEV1 was 7.2. Can you help me think through questions about hypothyroidism management and whether I need a referral to Central Texas Cardiology given my age and risk factors?
Assistant: I can help — this is a good set of things to prepare before your annual physical. A few quick clarifying questions first so my suggestions are accurate:
- Is your FEV1 7.2 liters or 72% (or 7.2 L/s)? 7.2 L is unusually large for FEV1, so I want to make sure I interpret it correctly.  
- Do you already have a diagnosis of hypothyroidism and are you taking levothyroxine (or any thyroid medication) now?  
- When you say “Central Texas Cardiology,” did you mean a specific clinic (and is it local to you), or did you mean a local cardiology practice in Seattle? (If it’s remote, that affects referral practicality.)

While you answer, here are concrete, practical things to think about and ask your PCP regarding hypothyroidism management and cardiology referral.

Questions & items to cover about hypothyroidism
- Current status & labs
  - “When was my last TSH and free T4? Can we check TSH and free T4 today?” (TSH is the primary screening/monitoring test.)
  - Consider anti-TPO antibodies if autoimmune thyroiditis is suspected or if it would change management.
- Symptoms and goals
  - Review symptoms (fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, hair thinning, cognitive slowing) and whether they might be from thyroid dysfunction vs. other causes (COPD, medications, etc.).
  - Ask what TSH target is appropriate for you given your age and cardiac risk factors.
- Medication management & interactions
  - If you’re on levothyroxine: confirm dosing/time of day (take levothyroxine on an empty stomach 30–60 minutes before eating), and review interactions (avoid calcium, iron, some antacids within 4 hours; separate from soy, certain supplements).
  - Discuss how to adjust dose safely: if you have known cardiovascular disease or significant risk factors, endocrinologists/PCPs often “start low and go slow” to avoid cardiac strain from excess thyroid hormone.
  - Ask whether any of your current meds (losartan, amlodipine, naproxen PRN) need special consideration — generally they don’t interact strongly with levothyroxine, but it’s worth confirming.
- Effects on other health issues
  - Ask how treating hypothyroidism could affect your cholesterol — hypothyroidism often raises LDL; treatment can improve lipids.
  - Because you have nephropathy, ask whether kidney function changes could affect thyroid test interpretation or levothyroxine dosing (severe CKD can alter thyroid hormone metabolism; your PCP will consider BMP/creatinine).
- Monitoring interval
  - If dose is changed, ask to recheck TSH in 6–8 weeks (typical) and then adjust as needed.
  - If stable, typical monitoring is every 6–12 months, but frequency may change with symptoms or other med changes.
- When to consider endocrinology referral
  - Unclear diagnosis, unusual labs (discordant TSH and free T4), difficult-to-control symptoms despite normal labs, or need for complex dose management → consider referral to endocrinology.

Tests you may want to request at the visit
- TSH and free T4 (baseline and on any dose change)
- Anti-TPO antibodies (if etiology is unclear)
- Lipid panel (if not done recently)
- BMP/creatinine and urine albumin (given nephropathy)
- ECG if you’re starting or increasing levothyroxine and/or if you have cardiac symptoms or known disease
- Any other routine annual labs your PCP recommends (A1c, CBC) based on history

Cardiology referral — factors to consider
- Why you might need cardiology sooner:
  - New or worsening cardiac symptoms: chest pain, new/worse shortness of breath at rest or with minimal exertion beyond COPD baseline, palpitations, syncope, new leg swelling.
  - Abnormal screening tests: abnormal ECG, high-risk stress test, abnormal echocardiogram, markedly abnormal lipids despite therapy, or poorly controlled blood pressure despite multiple meds.
  - If you have established coronary artery disease, heart failure, significant arrhythmias, or plan for noncardiac surgery with uncertain cardiac risk.
- Why PCP management may be fine:
  - If you have no cardiac symptoms, a normal ECG, and your BP, lipids and risk factors are being managed (statin therapy as indicated, BP at goal or improving), primary care often continues risk management and only refers if issues arise.
- Given your profile (age 55, COPD, HTN on losartan+amlodipine, high cholesterol, nephropathy):
  - You have elevated cardiovascular risk. It’s reasonable to ensure you have a current baseline ECG and an up-to-date lipid management plan (statin intensity based on ASCVD risk). Ask your PCP to calculate your 10-year ASCVD risk if it hasn’t been done recently.
  - Consider referral if ASCVD risk is high, if you have symptoms, or if your PCP wants a cardiology opinion on starting or intensifying therapy, or before major procedures.
- Practical tests to request now (before deciding on referral)
  - Resting 12‑lead ECG
  - Lipid panel (fasting or nonfasting per clinic policy)
  - Basic metabolic panel (kidney function; important for medication decisions)
  - If symptoms or abnormal ECG: echocardiogram and/or exercise or pharmacologic stress testing as indicated

Specific phrasing you can use at the visit
- For hypothyroidism:
  - “Can we check TSH and free T4 today? If my TSH is outside the target, how would you adjust levothyroxine and when should we recheck?”
  - “Given my age and cardiac risk, what TSH target do you recommend? Should we start low and increase gradually?”
  - “Can you review interactions with my meds and supplements and advise on timing for levothyroxine?”
- For cardiology referral:
  - “Given my age (55) and risk factors — HTN, high cholesterol, COPD, and nephropathy — should I have a cardiology referral or any baseline cardiac testing (ECG, echo, stress test) now?”
  - “Can we calculate my 10‑year ASCVD risk and review whether my cholesterol and BP management are optimized or if referral is recommended?”

Safety and urgent signs
- If you develop chest pain, pressure, new severe shortness of breath, fainting, or sudden palpitations, seek urgent care or call emergency services — don’t wait for the appointment.

Would you like me to:
- Draft a short message/email you can send to Dr. Maria Santos summarizing these questions and requesting TSH/free T4, ECG, lipid panel and ASCVD risk calculation?  
- Or draft a quick checklist you can bring to the appointment?

Also please clarify the FEV1 number and whether “Central Texas Cardiology” is local/intentional so I can tailor the referral advice.
